new_statements.quote: Awara stress, as in many Papuan languages (Foley 1986:63–64), is a pitch accent system. Acoustic correlates to Awara stress generally are falling pitch and high intensity. [...] Awara has one main stress pattern with two alternate patterns. The main stress pattern has stress on the first and third (alternating) syllables, with primary stress falling on the last stressed syllable, as shown in Table 4.1. [Table 4.1: /ayi/ [á.yi] 'grandmother'; /bela/ [bé.la] 'female'; /gʌpmayi/ [gʌ̀p.ma.yí] 'hole'; /banipʌmin/ [bà.nip.ʌ́.min] 'believer'; /gusikayi/ [gù.si.ká.yi] 'sun'] [...] All syllables are parsed into binary units called metrical feet starting from left to right [...] The metrical foot is left-headed (trochaic) [...] Line 1 is unbounded (forms one upper foot) and is right-headed (iambic).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees exactly with the catalog rule 10 / 001 / 0010 / 00001.. (primary stress on the rightmost odd-numbered syllable): the book's left-to-right trochaic parse with a right-headed unbounded upper foot generates precisely that string for every length, and Table 4.1 instantiates 10, 001 and 0010 ([á.yi], [gʌ̀p.ma.yí], [bà.nip.ʌ́.min]). It refines the record with: secondary stress on the other odd syllables; the 'pitch accent' realisation (falling pitch + intensity); a lexical second-syllable-stress class; a ~22% class of disyllables with no dominant stress in isolation; phrasal clash deletion before monosyllabic verbs; quantity sensitivity only as a hypothesis for the neutral class. The unbou…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Binary trochaic feet are built exhaustively from the left edge over every syllable (a leftover final syllable forms a degenerate foot); each foot head is stressed and the rightmost foot head carries primary stress, the others secondary. So primary stress falls on the rightmost odd-numbered syllable: initial in disyllables ([á.yi]), final in trisyllables ([gʌ̀p.ma.yí]), third in four-syllable words ([bà.nip.ʌ́.min], [gù.si.ká.yi]). Stress is realised as falling pitch plus high intensity, which the author calls a pitch accent system; extrametricality is off. The pattern is affected across word boundaries: before a following monosyllabic verb the noun's primary stress is deleted by right-to-left clash removal ([gʌ̀p.ma.yi ɡʌ́t] 'I saw the hole'), so the domain is a phonological word larger than the syntactic word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, explicit: 'Line 1 is not conflated (removed), so the stress on the left remains as secondary stress' (p.40); parameter 8 'Line Conflation: off (secondary stress)' (p.44). Secondary stress on the non-final odd syllables, e.g. [gʌ̀p.ma.yí], [bà.nip.ʌ́.min], [gù.si.ká.yi].
new_statements.exceptions: (a) §4.2 p.41: a second pattern in 'some two- and three-syllable words in which stress occurs on the second syllable', analysed as lexically marked stress: /damé/ [da.mé] 'cliff', /butáyʌ/ [bu.tá.yʌ] 'sorry', /gutóŋʌ/ [gu.tó.ŋʌ] 'crooked'; before a monosyllabic verb these shift to first-syllable stress ([dà.me ɡʌ́t]). (b) §4.3 pp.42-43: stress-neutral words, 'only occurs with some two-syllable words in isolation. On these words there is no dominant stress. About 22% of the data analysed for stress does not exhibit prominent stress in isolation', e.g. /gokŋot/ 'mushroom', /bʌbʌm/ 'bamboo leaf', /apʌk/ 'tongs'; in a clause they take secondary stress on the first syllable and primary on the last syllable of the utterance; a heavy-syllable (CVC) hypothesis covers about half of them. (c) §4.1 p.40: primary stress of 3-syllable words is deleted before a following one-syllable verb (stress clash removal, right to left, delete left). (d) §4.4 p.44 parameter 5: 'Relevance of weight: quantity sensitive (lexical and heavy stress scheme)'. Footnote 4 p.43: stress-neutral words also exist in Nankina and Irumu.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2011 book (and so the 2003 phonology thesis it revises) 'focuses on the Awara dialect spoken in the Central region and more specifically, the Tawaya village variant' (§1.2 'Language and dialect', pp.5-6), based on data collected at the hamlet of Guninggwan from July 1994 to April 2003 (§1.3 Methodology). The authors group Awara into Southern, Central and Northern dialects, with the Southern dialect (McElhanon's 'Leron') differing more in phonology; the stress description is therefore for Central Awara.
